To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the DNA histograms of formalin-fixed par affin-embedded tissue can be corrected for DNA debris using a mathematical model that is based on random sectioning of nuclei.

(i) the debris in DNA histograms from paraffin- embedded tissues is generated from the nuclei of cells by random sectioning, (ii) the debris can be described as a Poisson distribution of fragment lengths, and (iii) the debris distribution is dependent on the size of the nucleus.
the DNA histogram debris is composed of fragments of DNA that result from the sectioning of the tissue and that the amount of debris can be reduced by increasing the number of sections.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a mathematical model to explain the distribution of debris in DNA histograms from paraffin- and frozen tissue preparations.
the application of DNA histogram debris theory and its application to DNA analysis in paraffin-processed tissue samples.
the generation of DNA histogram debris from tissue preparations, its effect on SPF determination, and the compensation of this effect.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a significant difference between frozen and formalin fixed, paraffin embedded DNA histograms and this difference can be quantitated.

the DNA histogram debris theory provides a basis for compensation of debris in DNA histograms and that the compensation is applicable to both frozen and formalin fixed paraffin embedded tissue preparations.
DNA histograms obtained by frozen and paraffin-processed tissue preparations are equivalent.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the SPF values obtained from paraffin- embedded tissues are comparable to those from frozen tissue.
the DNA histogram debris theory can be used to compensate DNA histograms from paraffin- embedded tissue preparations.
a significant component of the DNA histogram debris is generated by random sectioning of the tissue.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the DNA histogram debris generated by the two tissue preparation techniques is not identical, and the DNA histograms from formalin-fixed paraf-fin-embedded tissue require a compensation to be used with the DNA histograms from frozen tissue.
the DNA histogram debris generated during tissue preparation is a function of tissue thickness, the number of sections taken, and the number of nuclei in the section.
the debris generated from paraffin- embedded tissue is not random and is predictable.
